title: How To Handle Sloppy Routines As The School Year Winds Down ol-year-winds-down/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin addresses the common late-spring problem of routines becoming sloppy as students grow fatigued and distracted near the end of the school year. Rather than recommending the usual fix of reteaching routines from scratch, he proposes a fresher approach: increasing the pace, or 'double-time,' at which students perform an existing routine. He explains that speeding up a routine—without running or abandoning manners—injects novelty, purpose, and urgency into something that has grown stale, counterintuitively producing better focus than slowing down, which is the instinct many teachers follow when things go poorly. Linsin walks through the steps: choosing the most emblematic struggling routine, modeling the faster pace, having individual students demonstrate it, then having the whole class practice, cautioning that this fix only applies if fatigue—not a genuine loss of classroom control—is the underlying cause.
points: Routines commonly become sloppy in late spring due to student fatigue, testing pressure, and anticipation of summer rather than a fundamental behavior problem.
Instead of reteaching routines from scratch, Linsin recommends increasing their pace ('double-time') to inject novelty and urgency into stale procedures.
Double-time does not mean running or abandoning courtesy—it means performing the same steps at a noticeably quicker tempo.
The teaching sequence is: choose the most emblematic struggling routine, model the faster pace, have individual students demonstrate, then have the whole class practice.
This fix is intended for spring fatigue specifically; it is not a substitute for addressing an actual loss of classroom control.
quotes: At this time of year it isn’t unusual for routines to become sloppy.
Now, normally we recommend reteaching routines at the first sign of trouble. We recommend modeling and practicing them as if it were the first day of school.
When you tweak a single component of a routine in a way that makes it feel fresh and different, it has an odd way of transforming the entire attitude of the class.
Now, it’s important to note that double-time doesn’t mean running. It doesn’t mean cutting in front of others, forgetting their manners, or racing to see who is first.
The truth is, in most classrooms routines are performed far too slow. And when a routine doesn’t go well, when students are distracted and unfocused, teachers tend to slow the pace down even more.
Increasing the tempo works because it infuses purpose, urgency, and novelty into something that has grown tired and stale.
